prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, opening the 10^-18 regime of frequency metrology

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the experimental Higgs discovery (B053) to optical lattice clocks (B002). The chair asked whether I would keep B053 first without a principled credit rule, and after the full exchange my honest answer is no. No member has offered such a rule, and I cannot construct one myself: founding leadership credits those who conceived and built the detectors, discovery-year spokespersons credit a different set, and analysis leadership a third, so each choice is a judgement about which of thousands of people the prize stands for. The science of B053 is unchanged and I still rate it the most consequential result on the list. But the citation is a statement about the people behind the discovery, and here I cannot make that statement defensible. B002 does not have this problem. The magic-wavelength lattice is a single original idea, Katori proposed and first demonstrated it, and Ye took the strontium clock to the 10^-18 accuracy and stability frontier. The result is reproduced and surpassed in several independent national laboratories, and it is used in tests of varying constants, dark-sector searches and relativistic geodesy. Five colleagues with different specialities independently reached this position, which I treat as evidence about the quality of the case and not as a count to follow. No two-part prize helps: B002 plus any second part would exceed the three-person limit or force a credit cut I cannot justify.
statement.case_against: My earlier objection to B002 was novelty, and I have not dissolved it entirely. The 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems cover much of the toolbox, and a sceptical reader can see lattice clocks as a spectacular refinement of an already honoured line. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the main practical payoff is still prospective. The Katori-Ye credit also omits Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the theory of Derevianko, and the split between the lattice concept and the long JILA programme is contested. I accept B002 because the other reservations I have are worse. B053 has an attribution problem I cannot resolve. B038 is conceptually attractive and cleanly attributed in theory but is about eight years old with an unresolved pairing mechanism, and its experimental credit leaves out Cao and the early authors. Choosing B002 is a judgement about which weakness is most tolerable, and I do not pretend the novelty margin is large.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the comb and ion-control prizes recognised enabling tools and a different system, whereas neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping is a distinct conceptual step that allowed 1e-18 stability through large atom numbers.
responses.response: This answers the chair's first question well enough to move me. The comb made optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions and photons. Neither contains the idea of cancelling the light shift of the clock transition in a lattice so that many neutral atoms can be interrogated together, which is what changed the statistical and systematic limits. I would state that in one sentence as the basis of the citation, and keep the wording on the lattice concept and its realisation, not on precision metrology in general. I also agree that his Hall-laboratory link should be recorded as a perceived connection and handled in procedure. I do not regard it as disqualifying, and I take his own question about abstaining as one for the committee to settle openly.

responses.point: Lindroth holds that the comb and ion-clock overlap is real but argues for careful citation wording and not demotion, and that the clock credit is concentrated on two people who conceived and drove the result.
responses.response: I accept this. I ranked B002 eighth partly because I weighted overlap with earlier metrology prizes too heavily. Her point that this calls for careful wording is right, and the citation I propose names the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice explicitly. On the Katori-Ye allocation against Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Derevianko, my view is that Katori's proposal and first demonstration and Ye's accuracy programme are the two identifiable load-bearing contributions. The others developed and refined them, which is a normal feature of a mature field and does not make the two-name credit unfair. On waiting for the redefinition of the second, I would not wait: independent confirmation at the 1e-18 level is already established, and awaiting a metrological institution's decision would make the prize depend on a process outside physics.

responses.point: Johansson says the Higgs attribution problem is not a footnote, that three individuals cannot fairly stand for a discovery made by thousands, and that he would not oppose it only if colleagues find a principled allocation.
responses.response: He is right and I have changed my position because of it. I had argued that a diffuse credit problem is a reason to choose names carefully, but the exchange showed that no choice among founders, 2012 spokespersons and analysis leaders can be defended as the discoverers, and the citation would then say more about institutional leadership than about the discovery. I also take his point that circuit QED has its own Blais versus Girvin squeeze and that the 2025 prize counts against it, so I do not propose B017 either. I would still welcome an alternative argument for B053 if anyone has a principled rule, which is why it remains my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B038 for a quantitative prediction followed by an experimental discovery, reproduced widely, with the stated weaknesses of timing and the unresolved superconducting mechanism, and said he could accept B002 as part of a two-part prize.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-then-discovery pairing is attractive and that the flat-band physics is robust, which is why B038 stays on my alternatives list. The chair asked whether the pairing mechanism can be left outside the citation, and it can, as Mehlig and Eriksson both word it. But the experimental credit problem is not solved by that: Jarillo-Herrero's group result carries Cao and other early authors outside the three seats. What would raise B038 above B002 for me is a few more years in which the mechanism or the main correlated states are understood and the experimental credit is clearer. On a two-part prize I do not see how to fit B002 and B038 within three people, so I would not propose it.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B038 organises a large phenomenology with a minimal model, with the broadest opening support, but concedes that if maturity outweighs breadth B002 is the safer choice.
responses.response: I find his concession persuasive on the criterion I weigh most. The conceptual economy of the Bistritzer-MacDonald model appeals to me as a theorist, and I would not dismiss B038 as a future prize. This year the safer choice on maturity and attribution is B002, and he says so himself. I would keep the B038 citation avoiding any claim to explain the superconductivity if it comes to a vote.

responses.point: Pearce argues that B002 is the only candidate six members placed in their top five, that the numbers are reproduced across laboratories, and that no statutory limit forces a leader out of a two-laureate prize.
responses.response: I agree with the substance and with his observation that two laureates fit this case naturally, which is exactly what the Higgs case lacks. I do not treat the breadth of support as a substitute for the scientific judgement, but his scientific points are the ones I would give: reproduction in several independent laboratories, a result that extends to geodesy and fundamental-constant tests, and a concept attributable to specific people. I also noted his point on IceCube and agree the diffuse flux is secure but the source picture is incomplete, so I do not move to B043.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the novelty margin over the 2005 and 2012 prizes as sufficient; I have accepted it, but a reasonable member could not.

Whether Katori and Ye fairly represent early lattice-clock credit, and whether I am underweighting Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow; I rely on general knowledge and have not verified priority details beyond the shortlist.
Whether a principled credit rule for B053 exists that I have not thought of; if the committee finds one, I would reconsider it as a lead.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second; I judge that waiting is not required, but this is a judgement about timing and not a scientific fact.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B002, B053 or B038. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is credited. My black-hole research is thematically adjacent to the Event Horizon Telescope (B051), with no documented link to its credited names, and B051 is not in my configuration. I note Kroll's disclosed perceived link to B002 through John Hall's laboratory and agree it should be recorded as such. I have no link to Katori or Ye.
